abstract: Perceptive locomotion policies typically observe a dense robot-centric elevation map, although only the terrain beneath and around the next footsteps informs the control decision. Learned encoders compress the whole visual input, leaving the policy to work out which inputs matter while learning the baseline locomotion task. Learning both at once slows training and, without computationally expensive attention mechanisms, makes generalization to new terrain harder. We instead remove redundant inputs from the elevation map before the policy sees it. A lightweight foothold prediction model (FPM) predicts future footholds from proprioception and the velocity command alone, and we sample the elevation map only in small patches around these predicted footholds. We train the prediction model alongside the locomotion policy, periodically retraining it on new policy rollouts as the robot’s gait matures. This allows the perception to anticipate where the policy will step, while the policy learns to leverage terrain information around those steps. With the proposed lightweight preprocessing, the policy reaches a given terrain difficulty in roughly a third of the training iterations required with the complete map. It outperforms policies that observe the complete map where footholds are sparse, including in narrow walled corridors, and on unseen terrain, and it matches an attention-based encoder trained at several times the cost. The policy transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid traversing various obstacles, stairs, gaps, and step-downs beyond the training distribution in both indoor and outdoor environments.

sections.body: The paper argues that dense elevation maps add redundant input, since only terrain near the next footsteps affects the control decision. Existing encoders still process the full map, and foothold planners run outside the policy. The proposed lightweight foothold prediction model (FPM) predicts the next footholds from proprioception and the velocity command alone. The policy then observes only elevation-map patches around those predictions. The FPM is trained alongside the policy and refit on new rollouts. The authors list three contributions: the self-supervised FPM, a gated perceptive pipeline with design insights, and simulation and hardware experiments against elevation-map encoders.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Predicting footholds from proprioception and filtering the elevation map around them should cut redundant input for perceptive humanoid locomotion.

sections.body: The task is formulated as a Markov decision process and trained with PPO across 8192 parallel environments in IsaacLab on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU. The controlled robot is a 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid. Physics runs at 200 Hz and the policy at 50 Hz. The system state is a 70-dimensional proprioceptive vector containing base velocities, projected gravity, the velocity command, and joint positions and velocities. The velocity command is resampled during training within -1 to 1 m/s forward, -0.5 to 0.5 m/s lateral, and -1 to 1 rad/s yaw rate. Two percent of environments receive a turn-in-place command and two percent a zero command. The exteroceptive input is kept separate from this state.
sections.heading: Preliminaries
sections.headline: The locomotion task is set as a reinforcement learning problem for a 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid trained with PPO in 8192 parallel environments.

sections.body: The framework has two learned parts: a foothold prediction model (FPM) that maps the 70-dimensional state to the planar positions of the next two footholds, and a locomotion policy. The FPM is an MLP with two hidden layers of width 128, trained with a Huber loss on footholds labeled from policy rollouts. Each predicted foothold selects a 7 by 7 patch of the elevation map at 0.05 m resolution, giving a 102-value height scan instead of 693 cells. During training, the sampled patches receive per-episode offsets between -0.05 and 0.05 m and per-point noise between -0.1 and 0.1 m. Every 500 iterations the FPM is retrained from scratch for 25 epochs. The first 500 iterations use footholds placed directly beneath the base.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: A blind foothold predictor is retrained periodically, and the policy sees only small height patches around its two predicted footholds.

sections.body: The authors compare the gated policy with five alternatives over five seeds and 1000 episodes per terrain, including full-map inputs, two partial-map samplers, and two encoder-based methods. Learning speed is measured by the terrain curriculum level. The gated policy reaches level 5 after 7.5k iterations, a speedup of 3.4 to 3.5 times over the full-map methods. The attention-based encoder AME2 ends marginally above the gated policy at 40k iterations but takes 6.3 s per update on four GPUs, against 0.55 s on one GPU for the gated policy. On the locomotion test, the gated policy scores 84.6% on training terrains and 83.1% on out-of-distribution terrains, close to AME2 at 83.6%. In the corridor test it scores 89.2% overall, the highest of the methods reported.
sections.heading: Experiments and Results
sections.headline: The gated policy reaches curriculum level 5 in 7.5k iterations, 3.4 to 3.5 times faster than full-map methods.

sections.body: The authors argue that the benefit comes from placing patches at predicted footholds rather than from a smaller observation, since sampling around the current feet or the commanded direction performs worse than the full map. The gated policy shows cautious behavior on hardware, which the authors conjecture comes from observations depending on the policy's actions. The stated limits are that full-map methods lead on stepped terrains, all methods perform similarly on continuous terrain, and the approach discards terrain the robot does not intend to step on. Obstacles entering from the side would reach the patches late or not at all, which the corridor walls do not test. The effective prediction horizon is limited to the second future foothold.
sections.heading: Discussion and Limitations
sections.headline: The approach trails full-map methods on stepped corridor terrain and cannot see obstacles approaching from the side.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the framework: a foothold prediction model trained with the locomotion policy predicts the next two footholds from proprioception and the velocity command, and the elevation map is sampled only around them. The authors report that the policy learns several times faster than full-map policies, matches an attention-based encoder at a fraction of its training cost, and performs best on most sparse terrains. It transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1. The stated future directions are an active depth-based perception system that observes predicted footholds directly, and manipulative locomotion that uses predicted hand and foot contacts to guide observation.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Sampling the elevation map around predicted footholds learns faster than full-map policies and transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1.
